en_summary: @aleabitoreddit argues that after the Lumentum/$MRVL deal, independent Western laser names $AAOI, $COHR and $SIVE became more strategically valuable, with $MTSI and $SMTC also in focus for 2027, while $AMD and others may rethink reliance on $LITE and chase vertical integration. $MRVL is framed as setting an M&A precedent rather than a fresh buy call.
text:
Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal: 

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable. 

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027. 

If I had to guess: 

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now. 

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".  

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use. 

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains. 

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company. 

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year. 

So M&A premiums likely went up. 

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expan

text:
Do CEOs still have to choose between coding and running the company?

Base's Jesse Pollak says leaders like Brian Armstrong, who write code and run agents themselves, are the only ones who can credibly tell their teams to push harder

"When I joined, I was writing code, and Brian still had like 60% of the commits and 60% of the code coverage."

"Some people love jumping on it, being like, why are these CEOs jumping in and writing code? I'm like, we were engineers first."

"You had to stop engineering because that was the only way, but now you don't have to stop. Now you can actually ship code and you can manage the organization using all these AI tools."

"Unless you have a leader like Brian or me who's in the trenches, writing code, running agents, trying to figure out how to make a swarm, you can't go and talk to your VPs or your directors or the team leads and be like, no, you can push way harder."

text:
Hello Monday!

This chart has been circulating on my timeline for the past couple of days.

In the Netherlands, employers are required to continue paying sick employees for 728 days. Almost TWO YEARS!

Second is Luxembourg, with just 77 days. A gap of 651 days!

Protecting sick employees is commendable and understandable. Sometimes things don't go your way.

But why put Dutch companies at such an enormous competitive disadvantage?

Sure, every country has its own system, so a one-to-one comparison isn't entirely fair. But a gap this extreme is hard to justify.

Why would any country choose this?

zh_summary: Agents are shifting roles from helpers to primary workers, turning people into managers of agent teams. Biggest impact on information-heavy jobs like coding, cybersecurity, legal, biotech, and engineering. Leverage decouples from hours worked as agents parallelize tasks, leading to compounding gains for early adopters.
en_summary: Agents are shifting roles from helpers to primary workers, turning people into managers of agent teams. Biggest impact on information-heavy jobs like coding, cybersecurity, legal, biotech, and engineering. Leverage decouples from hours worked as agents parallelize tasks, leading to compounding gains for early adopters.
text:
Increasingly this will be the new job description for a lot of roles, not just coding. We’re clearly moving from a world where agents help us do our work incrementally better or faster, to us helping agents do their work.

This turns everyone in one of these positions to that of a manager of a team of agents, instead of an individual contributor with just some added leverage from AI. The biggest areas of impact will be information-heavy jobs, like coding, cybersecurity, legal work, biotech, engineering, and many other fields. 

And as a result, in these jobs your leverage will begin to be decoupled from the normal ratio of hours spent working to output generated. For essentially the history of knowledge work the main variable you had to play with was hours of work done (assuming fixed level talent/coordination/strategy). 

Now we’ve separated these variables because agents can parallelize work for us, to in theory execute as much as we need to pull off whatever goal we’re trying to accomplish. The people and organizations that discover this sooner, and orient their operations around it, will see compounding gains in their workflows.

text:
I think AI compute cost-per-watt prices are going to stay elevated a lot longer than many people expect.

Less than 5% of U.S. consumers even pay a subscription for an AI product, with some putting the estimate <2%. People are clearly finding Grok Bot to be very useful because @SpaceX just had to significantly cut back usage capacity due to overwhelming demand. But we're still so early in the AI adoption curve.

Existing users are going to eat up significantly more compute as models get better and agents start handling increasingly complex tasks and jobs. Inference will increasingly become a larger and larger share of compute capacity.

People are seriously underestimating how much demand is still ahead of us and how long it'll take supply to catch up. I think this is partly why Elon thinks SpaceX could exit 2027 with an annual recurring revenue rate of $500 billion to $1 trillion. They can deploy the compute faster than anyone else, and the demand for that compute is insatiable, and likely will be for a long time to come.

The DRAM ETF was up 2.0% last week as an example while the SOX index was down 0.8%. 

My issue with the memory companies over a longer-term basis is over the next couple of years. China is bringing on a lot of capacity. CXMT currently has ~8% market share with a goal of 20% by 2028. Japan crushed the US memory companies in the 1980s when they entered the semi market. Korea crushed Japan in the early 2000s when they entered the memory market. From a pilot I trust:

It is too early to tell all of the factors that played a roll but likely complacency and inexperience. From the ATC audio tape and radar (see below) I would say inexperienced pilot or pilots and obviously weather. They likely flew into the storms and iced up.  

The Lear has a very critical wing and if they iced up in the thin air at altitude, they likely experienced a power on stall which can result in an upset and or snap roll.  As they asked to climb, we know they were likely at a very high power setting.  

Investigation should provide more insight as to whether they had the radar on or not and the training records as well as experience levels of the crew and any difficulty they may have had over the years with training. They will
also rebuild their days before the flight looking at any causal factors like fatigue.  

This should not have happened. I have a video of the impact and the plane appears to be intact just before impact. 

We absolutely would not cross a line of storms like that while descending into them.

$BX Blackstone COO Jonathan Gray: The economic value of computing infrastructure may increasingly support asset-backed financing independent of individual technology-company credit profiles.

"When you look at the airline business, lending against aircraft is an investment-grade business, not because Spirit Airlines or an emerging market airline has great credit themselves, but it's because of the shortage of commercial aviation in the world. Today, when it comes to compute, be it data centers or chips, people are not putting much value on the underlying assets. They're solely looking at the credit of the counterparties. I think that will evolve over time, which will expand some of the capacity these insurance companies have."

text:
UBS models $META Muse at just 3M daily users with number of $AMD EPYC chips required depending heavily on how many agents are running simultaneously and how efficiently CPU capacity is shared: 

• Base case ~3,000 chips if 750K agents run simultaneously with 4x CPU sharing
• High engagement ~23,800 chips if 1.5M agents run simultaneously without CPU sharing

But the bigger opportunity is what happens as adoption scales because same base assumptions would imply nearly 100,000 EPYC chips at 100M daily users while each Muse agent also requires its own 8GB of RAM and 100GB of SSD storage.

That could push DRAM requirements toward 2TB per host at 4x CPU sharing creating a huge opportunity for $MU and $SKHY in DRAM and $SNDK in NAND flash storage.

text:

How big is the market if good enough intelligence is very, very cheap?"
